stem: A Container App's managed identity must read secrets from Key Vault and nothing more. The vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Which role do you assign?

options.text: Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Secrets Officer
Key Vault Contributor
Reader on the Key Vault resource

explanation: Key Vault Secrets User grants get and list on secret values — exactly what an application needs and nothing more.

whyWrong.B: Secrets Officer can create, update and delete secrets, which exceeds read-only.
whyWrong.C: Key Vault Contributor manages the vault resource itself and does not grant access to secret values.
whyWrong.D: Reader is a control-plane role: it lets you see that the vault exists, not read its data.

stem: A high-traffic API reads an Azure OpenAI key from Key Vault on every incoming request. Under load, some requests fail with throttling errors from Key Vault. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Cache the secret and refresh it periodically
Create a second Key Vault and read from both in round-robin
Upgrade the vault to the Premium SKU
Increase the retry count in `SecretClient`Options

explanation: Key Vault enforces per-vault transaction limits and is explicitly documented as a secret store, not a per-request lookup service. Caching the value with periodic refresh — and re-fetching when a call is rejected as unauthorised — is the documented pattern.

whyWrong.B: Sharding across vaults is complexity to work around a design flaw the cache removes.
whyWrong.C: Premium adds HSM-backed keys. It does not change secret throttling limits.
whyWrong.D: More retries against a throttled service extends latency and keeps the pressure on.

hint: Key Vault is a management-plane service with request limits; it was never meant to be on the hot path. What should sit between it and each request?

stem: Which statements about Key Vault soft delete and purge protection are correct? Choose two.

options.text: Soft delete is enabled on all vaults and cannot be disabled
Once purge protection is enabled it cannot be disabled
Purge protection is enabled by default on new vaults
Soft delete only applies to the vault, not to individual secrets
Soft-deleted secrets are purged immediately by an admin

explanation: Soft delete is mandatory and always on. Purge protection is optional but irreversible once enabled — that is the point, since it stops an attacker or a mistake from permanently destroying secrets before the retention period elapses.

whyWrong.C: Purge protection is opt-in.
whyWrong.D: Soft delete covers vaults and the objects inside them — secrets, keys and certificates.
whyWrong.E: With purge protection on, nobody can purge early; the object is removed only after the retention period.

stem: You want applications to pick up a rotated secret automatically, without a redeployment or a configuration change. How should the secret be referenced?

options.text: By a versionless secret URI in the reference
By the full URI including the specific version identifier
By copying the value into an app setting during each deployment
By storing the secret in App Configuration instead

explanation: Omitting the version from the secret URI makes Key Vault return the current version. Rotation then becomes transparent — the app reads the new value on its next fetch or refresh.

whyWrong.B: A pinned version keeps returning the old secret after rotation, which is precisely the failure mode to avoid.
whyWrong.C: This ties rotation to the deployment cycle and puts the secret value into configuration.
whyWrong.D: App Configuration is for non-secret settings; it can hold a Key Vault reference, but the versionless URI is still what makes rotation transparent.

stem: You must be notified before a stored credential expires so an automated job can rotate it. Which mechanism does Key Vault provide?

options.text: A rotation policy raising SecretNearExpiry
A diagnostic setting that logs secret reads to Log Analytics
An Azure Monitor metric alert on vault availability
A soft-delete retention alert on the vault

explanation: Key Vault publishes lifecycle events to Event Grid, including SecretNearExpiry and SecretExpired. A rotation policy sets the notification window, and a Function subscribing to the event performs the rotation.

whyWrong.B: Read auditing tells you who accessed a secret, not that it is about to expire.
whyWrong.C: Availability metrics describe the service, not the objects in it.
whyWrong.D: Soft-delete retention concerns deleted objects, not expiring ones.

hint: Key Vault can tell you a credential is nearing expiry, and that notice has to travel somewhere an automation can subscribe to.

stem: The same code must authenticate to Azure services on a developer laptop and in Azure with a user-assigned managed identity. Which credential type do you use, and what extra detail is required in Azure?

options.text: `DefaultAzureCredential`, passing the managed identity's client id in the options
`ManagedIdentityCredential` only, which also works locally
`ClientSecretCredential` with the secret stored in Key Vault
`DefaultAzureCredential` with no configuration, which detects user-assigned identities automatically

explanation: `DefaultAzureCredential` tries a chain — environment, workload identity, managed identity, developer tooling such as the Azure CLI — so the same code works in both places. A user-assigned identity is ambiguous when several are attached, so its client id must be supplied.

whyWrong.B: ManagedIdentityCredential has nothing to authenticate against on a laptop.
whyWrong.C: This reintroduces a secret, and bootstrapping it from Key Vault needs a credential anyway.
whyWrong.D: The system-assigned identity is found automatically, but a user-assigned one must be identified explicitly.

stem: One App Configuration store holds settings for dev, test and production. How do you keep the same key names while returning different values per environment?

options.text: Give each value an environment label and select it
Prefix each key with the environment name
Create a separate App Configuration store per environment
Use a separate feature flag per environment

explanation: Labels are the dimension App Configuration provides for exactly this. The same key exists once per label, and the app selects its label at startup.

whyWrong.B: Prefixing works but changes the key names, and label filtering exists precisely to avoid that.
whyWrong.C: Valid for strong isolation, but the question asks how to do it within one store.
whyWrong.D: Feature flags toggle behaviour on and off; they are not a mechanism for environment-specific values.

docs.title: Keys and values in App Configuration

stem: A service must pick up App Configuration changes without a restart, and must never observe a half-applied set of related settings. How do you configure refresh?

options.text: Register a sentinel key and update it last
Register every key for refresh with a short cache expiration
Poll the store on a timer and rebuild the configuration root
Enable geo-replication so changes propagate atomically

explanation: The sentinel key pattern makes one key the trigger: the provider only watches that key, and reloads everything when it changes. Updating it last means the reload sees a complete, consistent set.

whyWrong.B: Watching every key means each poll can catch a partially applied batch, which is the inconsistency being avoided — and it multiplies requests.
whyWrong.C: Hand-rolled polling duplicates what the provider does and still has the consistency problem.
whyWrong.D: Geo-replication concerns availability and latency across regions, not update atomicity for a reader.

hint: The problem is a partial read while several keys are mid-update. You need one key whose change signals that the whole set is now consistent.

stem: A new ranking algorithm must be enabled for 10% of users, with the ability to turn it off instantly if quality drops. What do you implement?

options.text: A feature flag with a percentage filter
A deployment slot swap with 10% traffic routing
An environment variable set on 10% of instances
A Key Vault secret holding the rollout percentage

explanation: Feature management with a percentage filter is designed for gradual rollout, and toggling the flag takes effect without redeploying. Instant rollback is the deciding requirement.

whyWrong.B: Slot traffic routing splits at the instance level, not per user, and rolling back means another swap.
whyWrong.C: Per-instance variables give inconsistent behaviour for the same user across requests.
whyWrong.D: Key Vault stores secrets; a rollout percentage is neither secret nor a feature-management mechanism.

stem: Your app reads both plain settings and secrets. You want one configuration source in code, with secrets still stored in Key Vault. What do you do?

options.text: Store Key Vault references in App Configuration
Copy the secret values into App Configuration as regular key-values
Store all plain settings in Key Vault alongside the secrets
Read App Configuration at startup and Key Vault on each request

explanation: App Configuration can hold a Key Vault reference, which the provider resolves by calling Key Vault with the app's identity. The application sees one configuration source; secret values never live in App Configuration.

whyWrong.B: This puts secret material in a store that is not designed for it and loses Key Vault's auditing and rotation.
whyWrong.C: Key Vault is not a general configuration store and charges per transaction.
whyWrong.D: Per-request Key Vault calls are the throttling anti-pattern.

docs.title: Use Key Vault references in App Configuration

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes system-assigned from user-assigned managed identities?

options.text: System-assigned is tied to one resource; user-assigned is shared
System-assigned can be shared; user-assigned cannot
Only user-assigned identities can be granted Azure RBAC roles
System-assigned identities require a client secret to be rotated every 90 days

explanation: A system-assigned identity shares the lifecycle of its resource. A user-assigned identity exists independently, can be attached to many resources, and keeps its role assignments when a resource is recreated — which is why it suits scale sets and repeated deployments.

whyWrong.B: This is exactly backwards.
whyWrong.C: Both kinds are Entra ID service principals and can hold role assignments.
whyWrong.D: Managed identities have no secrets to rotate; credential management is handled by the platform.

stem: A Function app with a managed identity must send messages to a Service Bus queue. Which role assignment is required, and at what scope should it be granted?

options.text: Azure Service Bus Data Sender, scoped to the queue
Azure Service Bus Data Owner, scoped to the namespace
Contributor, scoped to the resource group
Azure Service Bus Data Receiver, scoped to the namespace

explanation: Data Sender grants send only, and scoping it to the individual queue is the narrowest scope that works. Data-plane roles can be assigned at namespace, queue or topic level.

whyWrong.B: Data Owner includes manage and receive rights the app does not need, and namespace scope is broader than required.
whyWrong.C: Contributor is a control-plane role and does not grant data-plane send rights.
whyWrong.D: Data Receiver grants receive, not send.

stem: A GitHub Actions workflow must deploy to Azure without any stored secret. What do you configure?

options.text: Workload identity federation with an OIDC trust
A service principal client secret stored as a GitHub secret
A publish profile downloaded from the App Service
A SAS token scoped to the deployment container

explanation: Workload identity federation lets GitHub's OIDC token be exchanged for an Azure access token. The trust relationship is configured on the app registration, and no credential is stored in the repository.

whyWrong.B: This is a stored secret, which the requirement excludes.
whyWrong.C: A publish profile contains credentials.
whyWrong.D: A SAS token is a stored credential and does not authorise a deployment.

hint: The workflow can prove who it is with a signed token from GitHub. Something on the Entra side has to be configured to trust that token.

stem: Which single line wires an ASP.NET Core service up to Application Insights using the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro?

options.text: `builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()`.`UseAzureMonitor()`;
`builder.Services.AddApplicationInsightsTelemetry()`;
`builder.Logging.AddAzureMonitor()`;
`builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()`.`AddOtlpExporter()`;

explanation: `UseAzureMonitor` from the Azure.Monitor.OpenTelemetry.AspNetCore package configures traces, metrics and logs together and reads `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING`. It is the current recommended path.

whyWrong.B: That is the classic Application Insights SDK, not the OpenTelemetry-based distro the exam objective names.
whyWrong.C: This wires up logs only, leaving traces and metrics unexported.
whyWrong.D: An OTLP exporter sends to an OTLP endpoint, not to Application Insights, unless a collector sits in between.

stem: Requests that cross from an API into a background worker appear as two unrelated traces in Application Insights. Which cause fits?

options.text: Trace context is not propagated across the hop
The two services use different Application Insights sampling rates
The worker sets a different `service.name` resource attribute
The worker exports metrics but not logs

explanation: Correlation depends on the W3C `traceparent` value travelling with the call. A hand-constructed HttpClient outside the instrumented pipeline, or a queue message that does not carry the context, breaks the chain and the worker starts a fresh trace.

whyWrong.B: Sampling can drop spans but does not reassign surviving ones to a different trace.
whyWrong.C: service.name sets cloud_RoleName and separates the nodes on the application map — the trace still spans both.
whyWrong.D: Signal selection does not affect trace identity.

hint: Two unrelated traces means the correlation identifier did not survive the hop. Ask what carries it, and whether a queue message preserves it.

stem: In OpenTelemetry terms, what is the relationship between a trace and a span?

options.text: A trace is one operation composed of spans
A span contains multiple traces, one per service
A trace is a log line and a span is its severity
They are interchangeable names for the same object

explanation: A trace is the whole request as it moves through the system; spans are the individual operations inside it, linked by parent-child relationships and sharing a trace id.

whyWrong.B: The containment is the other way around.
whyWrong.C: Neither term refers to log severity.
whyWrong.D: They are distinct concepts with distinct identifiers.

stem: You want to time the embedding step of a request as its own span within the existing trace. What do you use in .NET?

options.text: An `ActivitySource` starting an Activity
A Stopwatch, logging the elapsed milliseconds
A custom metric emitted with a Meter
An ILogger scope around the call

explanation: In .NET, Activity is the implementation of an OpenTelemetry span. Starting an Activity from a registered `ActivitySource` creates a child span in the current trace, with its own timing and attributes.

whyWrong.B: A stopwatch measurement in a log line is not a span and will not appear in the end-to-end transaction view.
whyWrong.C: A metric aggregates values over time; it cannot show this step inside one request's trace.
whyWrong.D: A log scope adds properties to log entries but creates no span.

stem: Application Insights ingestion costs have grown beyond budget, but you must keep end-to-end traces usable for the requests you do keep. What do you configure?

options.text: Sampling applied to whole traces
A shorter data retention period
Disabling dependency instrumentation
A daily ingestion cap on the workspace

explanation: Sampling reduces volume while keeping sampled traces complete, so the transactions you retain are still fully diagnosable. Metrics are pre-aggregated so they stay accurate.

whyWrong.B: Retention affects storage cost, not ingestion, and does not reduce what you are charged to ingest.
whyWrong.C: Dropping dependencies cuts volume but removes exactly the spans that make a trace useful.
whyWrong.D: A daily cap stops ingestion once hit, leaving you blind for the rest of the day.

stem: Several microservices report to one Application Insights resource and appear merged in the application map. Which resource attribute separates them?

options.text: `service.name`, which maps to `cloud_RoleName`
service.version, which maps to application_Version
host.name, which maps to `cloud_RoleInstance`
deployment.environment

explanation: `service.name` becomes `cloud_RoleName`, and that is the field the application map uses to draw distinct nodes. service.instance.id becomes `cloud_RoleInstance` and distinguishes replicas of the same service.

whyWrong.B: Version annotates releases but does not split nodes on the map.
whyWrong.C: That distinguishes instances within a role, not the roles themselves.
whyWrong.D: Environment is a useful custom dimension but is not what the map groups by.

stem: You have the operation id of a failed user request and need every telemetry item from every service involved. Which query pattern gets there?

options.text: union requests, dependencies | where `operation_Id` == "abc123"
search "abc123" across all tables
requests | where id == "abc123"
`traces | where customDimensions.operationId == "abc123"`

explanation: `operation_Id` is the correlation field shared across telemetry types, so a union of the relevant tables filtered on it reconstructs the whole distributed operation.

whyWrong.B: search scans every column of every table — slow, expensive, and it will match unrelated text.
whyWrong.C: requests.id identifies one request, not the whole operation across services.
whyWrong.D: operation_Id is a first-class column, not a custom dimension, and this looks at one table only.

stem: Which change most improves the performance of a slow KQL query over a large table?

options.text: Apply the time range filter as the first operator in the pipeline
Move the time range filter to the end so other filters reduce rows first
Replace has with contains for text matching
Add a render operator to the query

explanation: Log Analytics partitions data by time, so an early time filter eliminates whole partitions before anything else runs. It is consistently the biggest single performance lever.

whyWrong.B: Every later operator would process the full history first — the opposite of what you want.
whyWrong.C: contains is a substring scan; has uses the term index and is faster, so this swap slows the query down.
whyWrong.D: render only affects how results are visualised.

hint: KQL evaluates the pipeline in order, so every later operator works on whatever the earlier ones left. Which filter discards the most rows soonest?

stem: Custom telemetry stores a tenant identifier in `customDimensions`. How do you group request counts by tenant?

options.text: `| extend t = tostring(customDimensions.tenantId) | summarize count() by t`
`| summarize count() by customDimensions.tenantId`
`| project tenantId | summarize count()`
`| parse customDimensions with tenantId | summarize count() by tenantId`

explanation: `customDimensions` is a dynamic column, so the property must be extracted and converted to a concrete type before it can be used as a grouping key. `tostring()` is the usual conversion.

whyWrong.B: Grouping directly on a dynamic property is unreliable and will not give the typed key you expect.
whyWrong.C: tenantId is not a top-level column, so project cannot select it that way.
whyWrong.D: parse works on strings using a pattern; it is the wrong tool for a dynamic object.

docs.title: Work with dynamic data in KQL

stem: Which query returns the slowest 10 dependency calls in the last day, showing the target and duration?

options.text: dependencies | top 10 by duration desc | project target, duration
dependencies | where timestamp > ago(1d) | `summarize` max(duration) | take 10
dependencies | sort by duration | limit 10 asc
dependencies | where duration > 10 | project target

explanation: top n by <column> desc is the idiomatic way to get the largest values, and it is more efficient than sorting the whole table. Filtering on time first keeps the scan small.

whyWrong.B: summarize max(duration) collapses everything to a single row, so take 10 has nothing to take.
whyWrong.C: This lacks a time filter and asks for the fastest calls; limit does not accept a sort direction.
whyWrong.D: A fixed threshold is not the same as the slowest ten, and duration is in milliseconds so 10 is a meaningless cut-off.

stem: Which table holds the stdout and stderr output of containers running in Azure Container Apps?

options.text: ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
ContainerLogV2
AppTraces

explanation: Console logs carry your application's own output. System logs carry the platform's messages about the app, such as why a revision failed to provision.

whyWrong.B: System logs are the platform's account of the app's lifecycle, not the app's output.
whyWrong.C: ContainerLogV2 is the AKS container logging table.
whyWrong.D: AppTraces holds ILogger output sent through Application Insights, which is a different pipeline.

stem: You need the 95th percentile response time per operation over the last six hours. Which query is correct?

options.text: requests | `summarize` percentile(duration, 95) by operation_Name
requests | where timestamp > ago(6h) | `summarize` avg(duration) * 0.95 by operation_Name
requests | where timestamp > ago(6h) | top 95 by duration desc
requests | where timestamp > ago(6h) | `summarize` max(duration) by percentile(95)

explanation: percentile(column, n) is the aggregation function for percentiles, and grouping by operation_Name gives one figure per operation.

whyWrong.B: Scaling an average has no statistical relationship to a percentile.
whyWrong.C: This returns 95 individual slow rows, not a percentile value.
whyWrong.D: percentile is an aggregation function, not something you can group by.

hint: You want one number per operation, so the aggregation needs a `by` clause. Ask which operator computes an aggregate over groups.

stem: Pods on AKS are restarting and you want the cluster events explaining why. Which table do you query?

options.text: KubeEvents
ContainerLogV2
AzureDiagnostics
Perf

explanation: KubeEvents holds Kubernetes events collected by Container insights — scheduling failures, image pull errors, probe failures and evictions. It is the equivalent of `kubectl get events`, queryable over time.

whyWrong.B: ContainerLogV2 holds container stdout and stderr, not cluster events.
whyWrong.C: AzureDiagnostics is a general table for resource diagnostic logs from many services.
whyWrong.D: Perf holds performance counters such as CPU and memory.

stem: Which pair of KQL operators lets you enrich request telemetry with matching exception records?

options.text: join kind=leftouter on `operation_Id`
union with a where clause on ids
mv-expand on `operation_Id`
lookup on timestamp ranges

explanation: A leftouter join keeps every request and attaches exception rows where the correlation key matches, so requests without exceptions are still returned.

whyWrong.B: union stacks rows from both tables; it does not correlate them into a single row.
whyWrong.C: mv-expand flattens an array within a row and does not combine tables.
whyWrong.D: Joining on timestamp would match unrelated records that merely happened at the same moment.

stem: An alert must fire when the failure rate of a specific operation exceeds 5% over 15 minutes. Which building block do you use in Azure Monitor?

options.text: A log search alert rule on a schedule
An activity log alert on the resource
A service health alert on the subscription
A workbook with a conditional visualisation

explanation: A computed ratio over a window is not a platform metric, so it needs a log search alert: the KQL query calculates the failure rate and the rule fires when the result crosses the threshold.

whyWrong.B: Activity log alerts fire on control-plane operations such as resource deletion.
whyWrong.C: Service health alerts report Azure platform incidents, not your application's failure rate.
whyWrong.D: Workbooks visualise data; they do not raise alerts.

stem: Which environment variable connects an instrumented application to its Application Insights resource?

options.text: `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING`
`APPINSIGHTS_INSTRUMENTATIONKEY`
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`
`AZURE_MONITOR_WORKSPACE_ID`

explanation: The connection string carries the instrumentation key plus the regional ingestion endpoints, which is why it replaced the bare instrumentation key. Instrumentation-key-only ingestion is retired.

whyWrong.B: The instrumentation key on its own is the retired mechanism and lacks endpoint information.
whyWrong.C: That points an OTLP exporter at a collector, not at Application Insights.
whyWrong.D: Not the setting the SDK reads.

stem: An application logs the full request body to help debug model prompts. A review finds customer email addresses in Application Insights. What is the appropriate remediation?

options.text: Redact personal data before it is logged
Shorten the workspace retention period to 30 days
Restrict access to the workspace with RBAC and leave logging unchanged
Move the workspace to a different region

explanation: The fix is at the source: do not emit personal data into telemetry. Access controls and retention are worthwhile defence in depth, but they do not address having collected the data in the first place.

whyWrong.B: Retention limits how long the exposure lasts, not whether it happens.
whyWrong.C: This narrows who can see it while the collection continues.
whyWrong.D: Region affects data residency but does nothing about the content being logged.

docs.title: Data collection and privacy in Application Insights
